name: Taiwan
sources: GDP $166.6bn and population 20.4m for 1990: Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics, Taiwan Statistical Data Book. Taiwan is not in the World Bank series because it is not a member, so the national statistics office is the source throughout this file.

interest_rate 0.0775 is the Central Bank of China rediscount rate, raised through 1989 to defend against the money-supply surge behind the Taiwan stock bubble and held into 1990. The commercial base lending rate ran around 10%.

The Taiex fell from 12,495 in February 1990 to 2,560 in October, an 80% crash. bubble is left at 0.0 because the model's bubble term is calibrated on Japan and a second hot start would be an invention, not a transcription; the crash is noted here as a known unmodelled fact.
Defence 4.9% of GDP: the ROC sustained one of the highest peacetime defence burdens in Asia against a claim on its entire territory.
Public debt near 9% of GDP: Taiwan ran a fiscal surplus for most of the 1980s and held the world's second-largest foreign exchange reserves in 1990.

authoritarianism 0.40: martial law was lifted in July 1987 and opposition parties were legalised, but the Legislative Yuan still seated members elected on the mainland in 1947 who never faced a voter, and they were not retired until December 1991. A liberalising one-party state, not yet a democracy.
separatism 0.05 is the independence question read from the inside — a live cleavage in the electorate rather than a territorial insurgency.
Military index 16: roughly 370,000 active, a large modern air force by regional standards, and essentially no capacity to operate away from the island.

What could not be verified against the roster's usual source, stated plainly. Taiwan is not a World Bank member and appears in NO World Bank series, so every figure in this file comes from the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics or from the Central Bank of China rather than from NY.GDP.MKTP.CD. The GDP figure was cross-checked independently at $166,622m for 1990 with a per-capita of $8,167, which agrees with what is entered. The CPI, the rediscount rate, the defence share and the debt ratio were not independently cross-checked and rest on the DGBAS transcription alone.

pop_growth_1990 = 1.1159%/yr. Taiwan is not a World Bank reporter, so the series above cannot be used. Population 19,069,000 in 1984 and 20,157,000 in 1989, compounded over the five years ending on the eve of the start date; figures from countryeconomy.com's Taiwan population table, which carries the Republic of China's own registered-population series. WEAKEST PROVENANCE IN THIS FIELD, STATED IN THE OPEN: this is the one nation of the 137 whose figure does not come from the World Bank, and the aggregator does not name its upstream source on the page. The corroboration is internal — the same table's 20,401,000 for 1990 is this file's transcribed population_m of 20.4.

note: 1990 TECHNOLOGY: AUTHORED, NOT DERIVED. What this nation knew on 1 January 1990 is transcribed and sourced grant by grant, exactly like every other 1990 figure in this file, and is not read off tfp_trend - there was never a code path from the trend to the known set, and the zero that stood there was a claim about the world rather than an absence of one (BIBLE section 8 and iron rule 4, both amended 2026-08-30). THE PREDICATE IS SPLIT, and split by the technology's OWN EFFECT TYPE so that it is mechanically computable and never a per-nation judgement call. A node whose effects include MilitaryEfficiency, MilitaryStrength, DiffusionEmission or CostReduction is SOVEREIGNTY-SIDE: holding it means this nation could PRODUCE it, so operating an imported article does not qualify. Every other node is USE-SIDE: deployed and in operational use here is enough, whoever built it, because the effect such a node pays is a productivity, health or output effect and that effect is real in the country where the machine runs. Of the 48 technologies the tree lets anyone hold in 1990, 17 are sovereignty-side and 31 are use-side.

ALL 48 OF THE 1990-ELIGIBLE TECHNOLOGIES WERE RULED FOR THIS NATION, one at a time, against a standard published per technology rather than per country. 6 were held and are listed below with their citations; 42 were refused. The refused ids are named at the end of this note so that a reader can tell a cell that was examined and refused from a cell nobody looked at - those are different claims and the schema would otherwise flatten them into the same silence.

Multitech (incorporated 1976, renamed Acer in 1987) shipped a 32-bit personal computer built on the Intel 80386 in 1986, second only to Compaq worldwide and months after the Deskpro 386 - Acer corporate history. Note that Taiwan's own fabs were NOT at this generation: see matl_semiconductor_lithography below.

Named fact, not the series: Taiwan is not covered by World Bank IT.CMP.PCMP.P2. Multitech - incorporated 1976, renamed Acer in 1987 - introduced a 32-bit personal computer using the Intel 80386 in 1986, second only to Compaq worldwide, and sold the first Chinese-language computer on a standard 386. A domestic 386 product line from 1986, four years before the start date, in an economy whose export industry was PC hardware.

Taiwan's Directorate General of Telecommunications introduced digital switching in 1981, which enabled touch-tone service and later vertical services such as call waiting and speed dialling; the DGT introduced cellular service in 1989 (company history of the Directorate General of Telecommunications, referenceforbusiness.com/encyclopedia.com). Taiwan is not in the World Bank series, so there is no IT.CEL.SETS cross-check.

Taiwan's Directorate General of Telecommunications introduced cellular service in 1989 and began setting up large networks in each of its major urban markets (company history of the Directorate General of Telecommunications, referenceforbusiness.com/encyclopedia.com). Taiwan is absent from the World Bank series, so there is no IT.CEL.SETS cross-check; the grant rests on the 1989 launch date alone.

Taiwan is not covered by WHO reporting and has no WUENIC value, so R1 cannot be applied; a named national programme is substituted. Taiwan launched the world's first nationwide hepatitis B immunisation programme in July 1984, initially for newborns of carrier mothers and extended to all newborns from July 1986, alongside a routine childhood schedule. The programme's effect was published by Chang M-H and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1997, reporting the fall in childhood hepatocellular carcinoma that followed it — the first demonstration anywhere that a vaccine prevents a human cancer. NOT a WUENIC cell: the evidence class differs from every other grant on this node.
